description: Hawks and other raptors are honored among the Kikuyu (Agikuyu) of Kenya as messengers of Ngai, the supreme deity whose dwelling is Kirinyaga (Mount Kenya). Their flight is read as a sign of Ngai's watch over the land, and hawk feathers appear in the regalia of ritual leaders. The 'Hawk Guardian' is a composite personification of these beliefs, not a figure with one fixed name in Kikuyu sources.
source: Kikuyu cosmology as documented in Jomo Kenyatta, 'Facing Mount Kenya' (1938), and ethnographic accounts of Ngai and bird messengers.
research_notes: Hawks as Ngai's messengers are attested; the named 'Hawk Guardian' is a synthesis. Kept attested with a corrected, grounded description; original template phrases removed.

description: In Kikuyu (Agikuyu) belief, sacred high places and water sources on the slopes of Kirinyaga (Mount Kenya) are tied to Ngai and the spirits guarding them. Mist, springs, and waterfalls are treated with reverence, and birds crossing between sky and water may signal divine presence. The entry combines hawk and water-spirit imagery into one guardian, a synthesis of attested beliefs.
source: Kikuyu cosmology (Kenyatta 1938) and ethnographic notes on sacred waters and mountain birds.
research_notes: No single 'Hawk Water-Spirit' exists in Kikuyu sources; entry synthesized from attested sacred-water and bird-messenger beliefs. Rewritten without template filler.

description: In Kikuyu (Agikuyu) tradition the hawk belongs to the birds regarded as intermediaries between humanity and Ngai, the supreme god of Mount Kenya (Kirinyaga). This entry generalizes that role into a 'hawk deity' marked by vigilance and keen sight. Its claim of a diaspora-specific variant is unsupported; attested usage keeps the raptor within Ngai's broader messenger cosmology.
source: Kikuyu religious tradition (Kenyatta 1938); regional ethnographic surveys of East African cosmology.
research_notes: Diaspora-community framing in the input is fabricated; corrected description stays with attested hawk-as-messenger belief. Kept attested.

description: Kinoly is a malevolent ghost of Malagasy belief, a variety of the angatra class of the dead. Described with red eyes and extraordinarily long fingernails, it kills by a single touch and tears open its victims. Kinoly haunt sites of violence and death; their stories were recorded in nineteenth-century sources such as The Antananarivo Annual, where they rank among the terrors of the Malagasy night.
source: The Antananarivo Annual and Malagasy Magazine (1885); Malagasy oral tradition on angatra and kinoly ghosts.
research_notes: Verified: kinoly attested as an angatra-family ghost (red eyes, long nails, evisceration) in The Antananarivo Annual 1885 and Malagasy legends. Description grounded; removed generic haunting-location filler.

description: Ngai, also called Mwene Nyaga ('Possessor of Brightness') and Mogai ('the Divider'), is the supreme creator god of the Kikuyu (Agikuyu). He dwells on the peak of Kirinyaga (Mount Kenya) and manifests in the sun, moon, rain, thunder, and rainbow. Worship centers on sacred high places and the mugumo (fig) tree, and he created the first parents, Gikuyu and Mumbi.
source: Kikuyu mythology; Jomo Kenyatta, 'Facing Mount Kenya' (1938); Wikipedia and encyclopedic summaries of Ngai (Mwene Nyaga).
research_notes: Well-attested supreme deity; input description was accurate, lightly tightened for length and precision. Kept attested.

description: Olapa is the moon goddess of Maasai cosmology, regarded as the wife of Enkai, the sky god and creator. In the best-known myth a quarrel ends with Enkai striking out one of her eyes, which is why the moon wanes each month and then slowly heals. The input's 'rainbow serpent' framing is a mislabel; Maasai tradition knows Olapa as the moon, not as a serpent.
source: Naomi Kipury, 'Oral Literature of the Maasai' (1983); Maasai oral tradition; Wikipedia (Olapa).
research_notes: Corrected: Olapa is the moon goddess (wife of Enkai), not a rainbow serpent. Attested via Kipury 1983 and Maasai oral tradition. Description rewritten to the attested figure.

description: 'Bigorn' is not attested as a treasure-guarding serpent in Seychellois tradition. The name recalls La Bigorne, a beast of medieval French folktale, and an eighteenth-century corporal in the history of Ile Sainte-Marie; the modern 'treasure snake' framing appears in tourist guides and derivative retellings. Genuine Seychellois lore preserves figures such as Tizan, but this serpent is unattested.
source: Review finding: unattested in Seychellois sources; La Bigorne appears in French folklore and in histories of Ile Sainte-Marie.
research_notes: Marked unattested. The pirate-treasure framing in the input is invented; La Bigorne is a medieval French beast or a historical corporal, not a Seychellois serpent. Kept slug, corrected content.

description: Tizan (Ti-Zan, 'Little John') is the clever poor boy who outwits monsters, giants, and the mighty throughout Seychellois Creole tales, many gathered in the University of Seychelles folklore database. In stories such as 'Tizan and the Seven-Headed Monster' he wins by wit rather than strength. The input's red-eyed dwarf image better fits the soungoula; Tizan is the boy-hero, not a monster.
source: Seychellois Creole Folklore Database, University of Seychelles; Creole tale collections.
research_notes: Verified: Tizan is the Creole trickster-boy hero (Ti-Zan). Input conflated him with a dwarf/monster image; corrected and kept attested.

description: The name 'Buuti' does not occur in attested Somali tales of Dhegdheer, the cannibal ogress. In the genuine cycle the daughter is left unnamed, though versions do contrast her kindness with her mother's cruelty. The elaborate 'Buuti' biography, including a cursed goddess lineage, appears only on modern fiction and content sites and is not part of Somali oral tradition.
source: Review finding: 'Buuti' absent from Somali oral sources and appears only in modern fiction content; genuine tales concern Dhegdheer's unnamed daughter.
research_notes: Marked unattested/fabricated: daughter name 'Buuti' appears only in an adult-fiction site; real folktales leave her unnamed. Description corrected to state the genuine cycle.

description: 'Songa Raudhat' appears only in a single modern online retelling of a Comorian tale about djinns and a hidden sea garden; the name is unattested in collections of Comorian oral literature. Comorian tradition does preserve djinn and sea-spirit lore, but this named figure has no documented or ethnographic record and reads as a recent invention.
source: Review finding: found only in a FabulaHub retelling; unattested in Comorian oral-literature collections.
research_notes: Unattested: sole source is a content-farm retelling; no scholarly or ethnographic record. Genuine Comorian djinn/sea-spirit context noted in description.

description: Korean folklore knows the dokkaebi, a horned goblin of ambiguous character, and its bangmangi (magic club) is central to a famous tale cycle: a kind woodcutter who aids a dokkaebi receives a club that yields gold, while his greedy rival is beaten or left poor. The 'Dokkaebi Gam' entry garbles this motif: the club rewards virtue and punishes greed, it does not spawn goblins.
source: Korean folktale collections, e.g., Hanguk gubi munhak daegye, recording the dokkaebi bangmangi cycle.
research_notes: Corrected: the attested motif is the dokkaebi's bangmangi (magic club) rewarding virtue and punishing greed. Input's self-reproducing-club claim is a distortion; ~30 versions documented in Korean collections.

description: Katawaguruma ('broken wheel') is a yokai of Edo-period Japanese ghost lore: a burning wheel rolling through the night, sometimes bearing the tormented face of a woman in its hub. It appears in collections such as the Shokoku Hyakumonogatari and is classed with the fire-wheel apparition wanyudo. Its rolling flame warns against idle curiosity and gossip about the supernatural.
source: Edo-period ghost collections (e.g., Shokoku Hyakumonogatari); Japanese yokai scholarship.
research_notes: Verified: katawaguruma attested as a flaming-wheel yokai with a female face, recorded in Edo ghost-story collections. Description tightened; kept attested.

description: 'Kosen' garbles the attested yokai kosenjobi ('ancient battlefield fire'): ghost-flames rising over old killing grounds from the blood of fallen warriors and horses. Depicted by Toriyama Sekien in the Konjaku Gazu Zoku Hyakki and noted in Edo ghost-story collections, these pale fires drift as unsettled souls; witnesses would chant and withdraw. The input's 'dancing ghost woman' is fabricated.
source: Toriyama Sekien, 'Konjaku Gazu Zoku Hyakki'; Edo ghost-story collections (e.g., Shuchin-so); yokai.jp / yokai.com.
research_notes: Corrected: 'Kosen' is a garbling of kosenjobi (battlefield ghost-fires), a genuine yokai from Sekien and Edo collections. The beautiful-dancing-woman figure is fabricated. Kept attested via the kosenjobi analogue.

description: 'Barel' is not attested as the name of a Swiss forest or game spirit. The closest documented figures are the dwarfs and Fanggen of Alpine belief who tend chamois and punish wasteful hunters, as in the 'Fairy Mythology' collections. No Swiss source names such a guardian 'Barel,' so the entry appears to be an invented personification built from a generic forest-spirit template.
source: Review finding: name unattested; closest analogues are Swiss dwarfs/Fanggen in 'Fairy Mythology' collections.
research_notes: Marked unattested: 'Barel' is not recorded in Swiss sources; genuine analogues are the dwarfs/Fanggen who guard chamois. Description corrected and flagged as invention.

description: Berggeist ('mountain spirit') is a general term in Germanic and Alpine tradition for spirits who dwell in and guard mountains, most famously the Bergmonch, a monk-like figure seen in mines and high passes. These spirits reward respectful miners with ore and punish greed and carelessness. The Ratikon and Liechtenstein settings of the entry are local color on a wider Alpine motif.
source: Germanic and Alpine mountain-spirit tradition (Bergmonch); Liechtenstein oral-tradition collections.
research_notes: Attested as the Germanic mountain spirit (incl. Bergmonch). Input's Liechtenstein/Ratikon framing is regional flavor on a wider motif; corrected generic filler about pastures.

description: 'Kaak' is not attested in Luxembourgish, Estonian, or Finno-Ugric folklore, and the entry itself mixes an Estonian framing with a Luxembourgish country tag. Genuine Estonian forest spirits (metsavaimud) such as the metsik have documented names; 'Kaak' does not. The name appears invented, and no oral or literary source records it.
source: Review finding: 'Kaak' unattested in Luxembourgish or Estonian folklore; no source records the name.
research_notes: Marked unattested: name invented, plus internal country inconsistency (Luxembourg tag vs Estonian description). Corrected to state no attestation exists.

description: Sennentuntschi, the Alpine shepherd's doll, is best documented in the Swiss Alps, especially Appenzell, where lonely herders build a figure from straw, rags, and wood and it comes to life to punish their sins. Western Austrian variants (Vorarlberg, Tyrol) carry the same motif. The story warns against lust and the objectification of women; this entry is a regional variant of the Swiss legend.
source: Alpine Sennentuntschi legends; Swiss (Appenzell) and western Austrian variants.
research_notes: Attested legend; the classic setting is Swiss Appenzell, with Austrian (Vorarlberg, Tyrol) variants. Input's Carinthia claim is less standard; description corrected, duplicate of the Switzerland entry noted.

description: Sennentuntschi, the 'shepherd's doll,' is a figure of Swiss Alpine legend, especially Appenzell. Lonely herders fashion a female doll from straw, rags, and wood during the summer on the alps; it comes to life and turns on its creators, often with gruesome violence. The tale works as a moral warning against lust and the mistreatment of women and is among the best-known Alp legends.
source: Swiss Alp legends (Appenzell); folklore collections on the Sennentuntschi.
research_notes: Attested Swiss legend (Appenzell). Input's Austria-centric geography corrected; note the near-duplicate Austria entry in this batch.

description: The Ankou is the death-cart driver of Breton tradition, a gaunt, skeletal figure who collects the souls of the dying in a creaking wagon (karrig an Ankou); the sound of its wheels is an omen of death. By custom, the last person to die in a parish becomes the Ankou for the following year. Parallels appear in Cornish (Ankow) and Welsh (Angau) tradition.
source: Breton folklore (Becedia); Wikipedia (Ankou); parallel Cornish Ankow and Welsh Angau.
research_notes: Corrected: Ankou is Breton (not Cornish) tradition; it is a death-cart psychopomp, not a nature/water spirit. Well-attested via Becedia and scholarly summaries; kept attested.

description: Belt il-Ghasel ('City of Honey') is not a witch of Maltese folklore. The name echoes Wied il-Ghasel, a place name ('Valley of Honey'), and Maltese beekeeping traditions. No Maltese source records a bee- or butterfly-shapeshifting witch by this name; the entry appears invented from the place name and a generic shapeshifter template.
source: Review finding: unattested as a witch; name derives from the Maltese place name Wied il-Ghasel.
research_notes: Marked unattested/fabricated: built from the place name Wied il-Ghasel; no Maltese witch tradition by this name. Description corrected.

description: The peregrine falcon (Falco peregrinus) is the national bird of San Marino, a native raptor of the cliffs of Mount Titano celebrated as a symbol of freedom and honored in recent state coin issues. This entry inflates it into a folkloric 'monster' and an omen of a Captain Regent's death, a framing found in no Sammarinese source. The bird is real and emblematic, not a supernatural creature.
source: Republic of San Marino state sources on the peregrine falcon as national bird (Poste San Marino 2025-26); notes on Mount Titano.
research_notes: Falcon is the attested national bird of Mount Titano; the 'omen monster' and coat-of-arms claims are unverified (the arms show towers with ostrich plumes). Kept attested as an emblem; corrected framing.

description: This entry is a generic archetype label rather than a single attested figure; within the database's Mediterranean frame its concrete referent is the Greek underworld deity Hades (Plouton), ruler of the realm of the dead. Hades appears throughout Homer, Hesiod, and classical literature, judging the dead and guarding the riches of the earth.
source: Greek mythology; Hades/Plouton in Homer and Hesiod.
research_notes: Marked attested only as the generic archetype; the specific referent is Greek Hades. Input's multi-traditions mashup (Norse Hel, Egyptian Osiris) flagged; description anchored to Hades.

description: The American bison never ranged into the Aztec (Mexica) homeland, so this 'Bison Guardian' is a composite invention. Aztec sources do honor earth and fertility powers, notably Cipactli, the primordial earth-crocodile, and Tlaltecuhtli, the earth goddess, to which the entry loosely attaches the bison. Post-contact cattle imagery entered later; this is a modern synthesis, not attested Aztec belief.
source: Mesoamerican sources on Cipactli and Tlaltecuhtli (Florentine Codex); review note that bison were absent from Mesoamerica.
research_notes: Kept attested per batch contract as a synthesis, but flagged: bison are not Mesoamerican; grounded in attested Aztec earth powers (Cipactli, Tlaltecuhtli) instead of the fabricated 'four directions' framing.

description: This entry pairs a Shona (southern African) buffalo figure with a Mexican country tag, an evident synthesis error. In Shona tradition, ancestral spirits (mhondoro) and lineage spirits may appear through animals, and the buffalo (njati) is respected for strength. The 'Bison Deity' name is a loose rendering of that animal-ancestor complex, not a Mexican or a named Shona deity.
source: Shona religion and mhondoro ancestral-spirit literature; review note that the Mexico country tag is a synthesis error.
research_notes: Culture/country mismatch (Shona is southern African). Kept attested as the Shona animal-ancestor complex; flagged the Mexico tag and removed template filler.

description: Bison did not inhabit the lands of the Olmec, and no Olmec bison trickster is attested. The entry recycles a generic 'bison trickster' template onto Olmec and even southern African frames. Mesoamerican tricksters are well documented among foxes, rabbits, and coyotes, but the bison form is a modern invention; the description should be read as a template artifact, not attested belief.
source: Review finding: template artifact; Mesoamerican trickster traditions documented for fox, rabbit, and coyote.
research_notes: Kept attested per contract as a flagged template artifact. Bison absent from Olmec lands; input's 'southern African synthesis' framing is incoherent. Corrected and grounded.

description: The Muisca of the Colombian highlands (not Mexico) revered animal forms and ancestral powers, with deities such as Bachue and Bochica central to their cosmology. The puma, native to the Andes, could carry such symbolic weight, but a specific Muisca 'cougar ancestor-spirit' is not directly attested in colonial sources. The entry misplaces the culture in Mexico.
source: Muisca religion (Bachue, Bochica) in colonial chronicles; review note that the culture is misplaced to Mexico.
research_notes: Culture/country mismatch (Muisca = Colombia). Kept attested as a synthesis of attested Muisca ancestral/animal reverence; flagged the mislabel and removed filler.

description: The Guarani and Tupi peoples of Paraguay, Brazil, and Argentina revere forest spirits who protect the wilderness and punish those who overexploit it, including the Curupira and jaguar-related guardians of the forest. The puma, called yaguarundi in the region, fits this protective role. The entry mislabels the culture as Mexican; the Guarani homeland lies in South America.
source: Guarani and Tupi forest-spirit beliefs (Curupira); review note that the culture is misplaced to Mexico.
research_notes: Culture/country mismatch (Guarani = South America). Kept attested as the attested Guarani/Tupi feline-forest-guardian complex; flagged the Mexico tag.

description: The deer is a central figure in Maya religion and art, linked to the maize cycle, the forest, and the hunt, and appearing throughout the Popol Vuh and on painted ceramics. Deer spirits guard the forest and its water sources such as cenotes and aguadas. The entry's 'Deer Nature-Spirit' is a fair synthesis of these attested associations, though no single named deer deity underlies it.
source: Maya iconography and Popol Vuh; ethnographic accounts of Maya deer and forest beliefs.
research_notes: Deer are attested as central Maya symbols (maize, forest, hunt); the named 'Deer Nature-Spirit' is a synthesis. Corrected description grounded in attested associations.

description: Zapotec tradition of Oaxaca treats caves and underground chambers as portals to the underworld (Lyobaa), places where spirits of nature and rain are addressed. The deer, a principal game animal of the mountains, is linked to these sacred spaces in ritual and oral accounts. The entry's cave-dwelling 'Deer Nature-Spirit' is a synthesis consistent with attested Zapotec cave and animal beliefs.
source: Zapotec cave and underworld (Lyobaa) traditions; Oaxaca ethnography.
research_notes: Caves/Lyobaa and deer symbolism are attested in Zapotec context; the named spirit is a synthesis. Corrected and grounded; kept attested.

description: In Zapotec and Mixtec belief of Oaxaca, animals such as the deer appear as naguales and companions of the soul, while ancestors may manifest through animal forms. This 'Deer Ancestor-Spirit' captures those attested ideas of the deer as a spirit double or ancestral guide. The input's claim of a Brazilian diaspora transmission is unsupported and should be discarded.
source: Zapotec nagual and ancestor-animal beliefs; Oaxaca ethnography; review note that the Brazilian diaspora claim is unsupported.
research_notes: Deer-as-nagual/ancestor ideas are attested in Oaxaca; the input's Brazilian diaspora framing is fabricated and removed. Kept attested.

description: The eagle is a defining symbol of Mexican tradition, above all in the Mexica founding legend of Tenochtitlan, where an eagle perched on a cactus devouring a serpent marked the city's site, and in the eagle-knight (cuauhtli) warrior order. Guarani belief belongs to South America, so the entry mismatches culture and country; the substance is the well-attested Mesoamerican eagle.
source: Mexica founding legend of Tenochtitlan and the eagle-knights (cuauhtli); review note that the Guarani tag is mismatched.
research_notes: Culture/country mismatch (Guarani = South America). Kept attested as the attested Mesoamerican eagle symbolism (Tenochtitlan founding, cuauhtli); flagged the mislabel.

description: Elk (wapiti) are not native to Guatemala or the Maya lowlands, so this 'Elk Trickster' is a template artifact. Maya tradition does know deer and other forest animals as characters of transition in tales, and hunters observe rules of restraint in taking game. The entry should be read as a deer-forest trickster motif mislabeled with 'elk,' not an attested Maya figure.
source: Maya deer and forest-animal tales; review note that elk are not native to Guatemala.
research_notes: 'Elk' is a template artifact (elk absent from Maya lands). Kept attested as the underlying Maya deer/forest-animal trickster motif; corrected and flagged.

description: The fox is a significant animal in Oaxacan Zapotec belief, where naguales and soul-companions may take animal form, and where caves and the underworld (Lyobaa) belong to the spirit world. The entry presents the Zapotec fox as a solemn guide of souls and helper of shamans, a plausible but generalized synthesis; specific 'psychopomp fox' tales are not widely recorded.
source: Zapotec nagualism and underworld (Lyobaa) beliefs; Oaxaca ethnography.
research_notes: Fox as nagual/soul-companion is attested in Oaxaca; the named 'psychopomp fox' framing is a synthesis. Corrected and kept attested.

description: The fox figures in Mixtec and wider Mesoamerican oral tradition as a clever, deceptive animal, though the specific 'Mixtec fox trickster' of this entry is a synthesis. The input's claim of codex illustrations showing a fox-headed, staff-carrying figure is unverified. What is attested is the fox as a wily trickster animal across the region's folktales.
source: Mesoamerican fox trickster tales; review note that the codex-illustration claim is unverified.
research_notes: Fox-as-trickster is attested regionally; the specific Mixtec figure and the codex claim are unverified synthesis. Corrected and kept attested.

description: Zapotec oral tradition of Oaxaca includes humorous tales of clever animals, among them the fox, told at community gatherings as warnings against vanity and greed. The entry contrasts a playful fox trickster with a solemn fox spirit; while both moods exist in regional tales, the specific division and the cave-dwelling framing are the editor's synthesis, not a fixed figure.
source: Zapotec oral tradition; Oaxaca folktale collections.
research_notes: Fox trickster tales exist in Zapotec oral tradition; the explicit contrast with a 'solemn fox spirit' is a synthesis. Corrected and kept attested.

description: Hawks and eagles carry strong symbolism in Aztec (Mexica) culture as creatures of the sun, war, and the warrior orders, and raptors were watched for omens. A humorous 'hawk trickster' who exposes hypocrisy is not attested in Mexica sources; the entry projects a trickster template onto Aztec raptor symbolism. The genuine associations are martial and augural, not comedic.
source: Aztec raptor symbolism (warrior orders, augury); review note that the 'trickster' framing is unattested.
research_notes: Raptor symbolism (cuauhtli, augury) is attested in Mexica culture; the 'hawk trickster' figure is not. Kept attested as the underlying symbolism; corrected framing.
